newsitem.title: UK: HK to succeed, China fears loss of face-negotiator.
newsitem.headline: HK to succeed, China fears loss of face-negotiator.

text.p: China will make a success of Hong Kong because failure would lead to a huge loss of face around the globe, a leading negotiator in the unique handover deal said.

Hong Kong's return to China on June 30 closes a major chapter in Britain's colonial history but Sir Robin McLaren is convinced one of the economic wonders of the world will still thrive under a "one country, two systems" government.

McLaren, former British ambassador in Beijing and political adviser to the Hong Kong government, argues that it is in the overwhelming self-interest of Communist China to ensure this monument to free market capitalism is not toppled.
"Think what a loss of face it would be if Hong Kong starts to go downhill rapidly," McLaren told Reuters in an interview.
"Of course China would blame Britain, the United States, anyone but itself. But the loss of face would be unbearable," he said.
Taiwan is also another crucial piece of the diplomatic jigsaw for China.
"Taiwan is waiting in the wings. The 'one country,two systems' formula was defined for Taiwan. This is the one piece of reunification business waiting to be done," argued McLaren.
"They have got to persuade Taiwan. The chances would be reduced to zero if they are seen to break all their promises in Hong Kong."
But McLaren, Hong Kong's chief political adviser from 1981-1985 and then ambassador in Beijing from 1991-1994, still has some political and economic qualms.
Hong Kong's Gross Domestic Product has almost doubled in real terms since Britain and China signed the 1984 Joint Declaration that gave Hong Kong back to Beijing after more than 150 years.
"The Hong Kong Special Administrative Region born at midnight on June 30 will be a highly privileged infant," McLaren said.
But he insisted: "The Hong Kong authorities will have to be firm in resisting people pushing for special deals.
"Hong Kong won't continue to be an effective international financial centre if people come to feel you have to have an inside track to do profitable business."
He also singled out freedom of the press and freedom of speech as serious issues to be addressed. "This is a slippery slope. If you start having self-censorship, when does it end?
"If people come to feel you cannot get up-to-date, swift and accurate information in Hong Kong, it becomes a much less attractive base for operations," he added.
China has fiercely resisted democratic reforms in the last years of British rule in Hong Kong and enraged democratic activists with its plans to roll back civil liberties.
But McLaren believes that Hong Kong's resilience and adaptability as an international money-making machine will triumph in the end.

"Over the last few years, there have been tremendous buffetings and fisticuffs with the Chinese all the time and what has happened to the economy? It has done extremely well and been pretty much the only bright spark in a pretty dull Southeast Asia."

Mclaren, going to Hong Kong for the handover after a 40-year involvement with the colony, said: "I shall be there among the spear carriers on the British side whilst the great and good are in the front row."
"But I shan't feel this is the end of everything. Hong Kong has been unique in the past and I don't see why it shouldn't go on being unique."
